title: Too little, too much water
text:
A story created @ Visualising Climate 2026, Bologna
Heat is the clearest signal in the E3CI, but water tells a more complicated story: months of drought and months of extreme rain, sometimes in the same country and in the same years. We follow both, from Europe down to Germany.

title: Too little, too much water
section: Europe
text:
Europe

Each hazard has its own story









Water extremes change less than heat. Since 2011 extreme precipitation has become about 1.5 times as frequent as in 1981–2010 (from 8% to 13% of the country-months), drought only slightly (from 13% to 15%), and the bars go up and down from year to year: wet and dry years alternate.


When in the year?









Look at the drought and precipitation roses. Drought grows above all from April to August (in April, from 13% to 20% of the country-months), while extreme rain grows in winter and autumn: in January, February and October, from about one country-month in ten to one in six.

title: Too little, too much water
section: Who is hit the hardest?
text:
Who is hit the hardest?

One month, all countries









Spring droughts matter for crops and rivers. May 2011 and May 2026 were extreme in 25 of the 45 countries, more than any other May. The countries with the most extreme Mays since 1981 are in the west of central Europe: Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Germany.


Too dry and too wet, region by region









Each dot is a month above 2 in one of the 15 German regions. Severe drought months went from 20 in 1981–1990 to 137 in 2017–2026; severe rain months increased too, from 81 to 110. The same regions now swing between the two extremes.


One map per year









Drought maps are patchier than heat maps: the large extreme Junes (1988, 2000, 2003, 2018, 2025 and 2026) are separated by years with almost no drought. In 2026, 21 of the 45 countries had an extreme June drought, the most in the series.

title: Too little, too much water
section: Zoom in: Germany
text:
Zoom in: Germany

46 years at a glance









One row per component, one cell per year. In Germany the drought row darkens in the same years as the heat row, such as 2003, 2018 and 2026: hot and dry summers come together. Since 2011, 21% of the months were in extreme drought, against 12% in 1981–2010.


Month by month









Drought values stay lower than heat values: in Germany the E3CI for drought has never reached 3. The three most extreme months on record are May 2011, August 2018 and May 2025, two of them in late spring.
Records tell a different story from frequency. The last drought record in Germany dates back to May 2011: since then droughts have been more frequent, but none has been more intense. A changing climate does not always mean a new record every year.


Which months, which years?









Before 2011 every calendar month was in extreme drought in at most one or two years out of ten. Since then May has been extreme in a third of the years and June in 40%: drought arrives when crops need water the most.


A real event: the floods of July 2021









Too much water, in the middle of a dry decade. In July 2021 North Rhine-Westphalia reached 11.5, its most extreme month for rain since 1981. The ranking on the right shows a shared event: Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands and Rhineland-Palatinate were hit in the same month.


Region by region









Extreme July rain is a regional affair: in most Julys it hits only a few regions. July 2014 (11 regions) and July 2021 (10 regions) are the exceptions, with two thirds of Germany at once. Berlin and Brandenburg are the regions with the most extreme Julys since 1981.

Data: E3CI – European Extreme Events Climate Index, https://www.climateindex.eu (IFAB; implemented by CMCC and Leithà – Unipol Group; distributed by Hypermeteo and Radarmeteo), based on Copernicus ERA5. Neither the European Commission nor ECMWF is responsible for any use of the Copernicus information. Colours: the E3CI Data Station palette (design by Cinzia Bongino). Country shapes: Natural Earth (public domain).

section: 0 · Setup ⏱ 3 min

0 · Setup ⏱ 3 min
Run these five cells once (click “Show code” if you are curious). Colab asks for two data files: in the second cell upload aci_comps_2026August.csv (the 51 countries, 2.4 MB), in the fifth one aci_comps_gaul_2026August.csv (the ≈750 regions used in Part 3, 35 MB). You can also drag both files onto the 📁 Files panel before you start, unless your organisers have already put a link in DATA_URL. The third cell checks the data and sets aside a few periods that look like processing gaps: real data always need checking before we draw them!



     
     
      Upload widget is only available when the cell has been executed in the
      current browser session. Please rerun this cell to enable.

title: Drought - test title
section: 1 · Europe: is it getting more extreme? ⏱ 8 min
text:
1 · Europe: is it getting more extreme? ⏱ 8 min
We count the country-months above 1: one country in extreme heat for one month = 1. With 45 countries and 12 months, a year has 540 country-months for each component.

1.1 Each hazard has its own story
One small chart per component (small multiples): every bar is the share of country-months above 1 in one year, the dashed line is the average of 1981–2010.









💬 Since 2011, months of extreme heat have been more than 3 times as frequent as in 1981–2010, and fire-weather extremes almost 3 times, while cold extremes and hail have become rarer. Precipitation, wind and drought change less, and less regularly: trends in these hazards are harder to detect than in temperature.
Now let’s look at the same hazards from another angle: when in the year do they strike?


1.2 When in the year?
A rose for each hazard and period, inspired by Florence Nightingale’s diagrams (1858). How to read it: * every petal is a calendar month: January at the top, then clockwise (April on the right, July at the bottom, October on the left); * the area of a petal, not its length, is proportional to the share of country-months that were extreme in that month, as in Nightingale’s roses; * inside each petal the classes go from the centre outwards: 1–2 (the lightest shade), 2–3, above 3 (the darkest); * top row: 1981–2010; bottom row: since 2011.
Remember: an E3CI “heat extreme” in January is an unusually warm January, not a 40 °C day.









💬 In 1981–2010 most roses are almost round: the E3CI measures every month against the same month of that period. Since 2011 the extreme-heat rose has grown in every direction: in every calendar month, from a quarter to almost half of the country-months were extreme, against about one in ten before. Fire weather grows above all in spring and summer (in April, from 5% to 20% of the country-months), while the cold rose shrinks, especially in summer and in late autumn.

title: Drought - test title
section: 2 · Compare countries: who is hit the hardest? ⏱ 7 min
text:
2 · Compare countries: who is hit the hardest? ⏱ 7 min
From here on, every chart looks at one component (or two) or at one place: in this guided tour we chose extreme heat, July and Italy, and the settings at the top of each cell can show any other.

2.1 One month, all countries
Extreme heat in July: every row is a country, every cell a year. On the right, how many extreme Julys each country had since 1981: the countries with the most are at the top.
Why July? It is the heart of summer, when heat extremes hit people the hardest. But the E3CI compares every July only with the Julys of 1981–2010, so any other month can be read in the same way: in the second part of the workshop you can choose it (MONTH = 0 shows the strongest month of each year).











2.2 One map per year
First we load the country shapes (Natural Earth, ~3 MB), then we draw one small map per year: small multiples let the eye compare 46 Julys at once.









💬 What do you see? Compare the first rows with the last ones: in the 1980s an extreme July was a rare, local event; since 2012 almost every July has hit large parts of Europe, some years in the north (2014, 2018, 2025), others in the south and in the Balkans (2012, 2023, 2024).

title: Drought - test title
section: 3 · One country, zoom in: Italy ⏱ 12 min
text:
3 · One country, zoom in: Italy ⏱ 12 min
After Europe as a whole, let’s zoom in on one country: the charts below show Italy and extreme heat from several angles, down to its regions. In the second part of the workshop you can choose your own country and component.

3.1 The barcode of extremes
Inspired by Ed Hawkins’ warming stripes: one row per component, one cell per year.











3.2 Month by month, as in the Data Station
Now one component only: extreme heat. Every bar is one month, coloured by E3CI class; the dots mark the three most intense months on record, with their value.









💬 The darkest bars, above 3, are almost all recent: 4 months in the 30 years 1981–2010, 30 since 2011. And the three most intense months on record are October 2023, April 2024 and July 2026 (remember: an extreme October is an unusually warm October, not a 40 °C day).


3.3 Records: are they falling faster than chance would predict?
The same months, seen through their records. A record is a month with a higher E3CI than every month before it in the same country, since January 1981. In a climate that does not change, records become rarer and rarer: after 10 years the chance that a month beats all the previous ones is about 1 in 120; after 40 years, about 1 in 480. That’s why we start counting in 1991: in the first years almost every month is a record, because there is hardly any history to beat.
📐 How many records should we expect? In a stable climate each of the first n months has the same chance of being the highest, so month n sets a record with probability 1/n. Adding up 1/n over the months since 1991 gives the number of records we would expect if nothing were changing. It is a reference, not an exact forecast: anomalies persist from one month to the next, so records can come in clusters.









💬 Since 1991 Italy has set 6 records of extreme heat, where a stable climate would give about 1.5, and 3 of them in the last ten years alone (April 2018, October 2022, October 2023), when about 0.2 would be expected. Every step of the staircase raises the bar, and yet the bar keeps being beaten.


3.4 Which months, which years?
The same data as a heatmap: rows are months, columns are years. Top: extreme months per year. Right: how often each calendar month was extreme, then (grey) and now (colour).











3.5 A real event: the Emilia-Romagna floods, May 2023
Many events hit only one region: here we use the regional data loaded in the setup. In May 2023 two waves of torrential rain flooded Romagna: was it the most intense month on record in Emilia-Romagna? How does it compare with the rest of Europe? The first cell lists other famous events: in the second part of the workshop you can choose one of them.

E.1 What changed?
All seven components for one country: the share of extreme months in 1981–2010 (grey) and 2011–2026 (colour). The title is written by the data: it names the component that increased the most.











E.2 Heat vs cold, region by region
In Italy as a whole heat extremes grow and cold extremes fade (see the barcode in Part 3): is it the same in every region? Here we use the regional data loaded in the setup. Each dot is a month above 2 in one of the 20 Italian regions: orange = heat extremes, blue = cold extremes; the bigger dots are above 3. The title is generated by the code from the first and the last ten years.

title: Heatwave in Sicily, July 2023
text:
A story created @ Visualising Climate 2026, Bologna
In the second half of July 2023 a long heatwave hit southern Italy: Palermo reached about 47 °C on 24 July, its highest temperature on record, and wildfires closed its airport. How extreme was it, and how does it fit into the last 46 years?

title: Heatwave in Sicily, July 2023
section: An overview of extreme weather events in Europe from 1981 to the present day
text:
An overview of extreme weather events in Europe from 1981 to the present day

Each hazard has its own story









E3CI tracks seven climate hazards, and they do not all move in the same direction. One clearly stands out: extreme maximum temperatures. Until the early 2000s the orange bars stay mostly below the 1981–2010 average; in the last fifteen years almost every bar towers above it, and the most recent years are the highest of the whole series. Wildfires, closely linked to heat, follow a similar path, with sharp peaks in recent years. Extreme cold and hail go the other way, becoming rarer. Drought, heavy rain and wind change much less. In short, heat has grown more than any other hazard, by a factor of about 3.5. This is why our story follows the heat. But when in the year does it strike? (2026 data up to September.)


When in the year?









In this plot is important to note that the area of a petal, not its length, shows the share: a petal twice as long means about four times as many extreme months. In 1981–2010 the rose for extreme maximum temperatures is small and regular, just above the 10% circle in every month. In 2011–2026 almost every petal reaches or exceeds the 40% circle, with no clear summer peak: February, April, October and November are as affected as July. On average, the share of extreme-heat country-months rises from 11% to 37%, and the dark outer band shows that many of them exceed E3CI 3. The opposite happens for extreme cold, which shrinks mostly below 10% (from 11% to 6.8% on average), and for hail (from 14% to 9.5%). Wildfires almost triple, from 5.5% to 16%, growing especially in spring and summer. Extreme heat is no longer a summer event: it is now spread across the whole year. But where in Europe does it hit?


Compare countries in Europe: who is hit the hardest in July over the years?









Until 2010, extreme Julys are isolated episodes, appearing only here and there. After 2010 the grid changes colour: extreme cells become increasingly frequent and, since 2022, almost the rule. Not all countries are affected equally: the Balkans and Central Europe top the ranking, and Italy, with 12 extreme Julys since 1981, is among the most affected countries. July 2023 was extreme in 18 of the 45 countries, fewer than in July 2025 (39), but it was one of the most intense in the south: above 3 in Italy, Malta, Greece, Albania and Croatia.


One map per year









Each map is a July, from 1981 to today: read it like a comic strip, left to right and top to bottom. In the first rows Europe is almost entirely grey, and extreme heat appears only occasionally. From the 2000s onwards the orange patches become more frequent, wider and darker, hitting different areas each time, from Scandinavia to the Balkans. Extreme heat is no longer a local exception but a phenomenon that moves and spreads across the continent.

title: Heatwave in Sicily, July 2023
section: Zoom in: Italy
text:
Zoom in: Italy

The barcode of extremes









One row per component, one cell per year. In Italy the heat row changes the most: 27 extremely hot months in the three decades 1981–2010, 84 in the sixteen years since 2011.


Heat and cold weather, region by region









The two indicators move in opposite directions: extreme events linked to high temperatures are increasing, while those linked to extreme low temperatures are becoming rarer and less widespread. The numbers make it clear: comparing the first and the last decade, extreme heat months rise from 95 to 703, while extreme cold months fall from 151 to 17. In the 1980s blue and orange dots alternate; today the chart is almost entirely orange, in all 20 regions.


Month by month, and the records









Top: only 4 months above 3 in 1981–2010, 31 since 2011. Bottom: Italy has set six heat records since 1991, where a stable climate would give about 1.5. July 2023 reached 6.2 for Italy as a whole, the second most extreme July, but not a record: October 2022 and October 2023 were even further from normal for their season.


The event: Sicily, July 2023









Sicily reached 13.5 in July 2023, its second most extreme July after July 2026 and its third most extreme month since 1981. On the right, the most affected regions of Europe that month: only Campania was higher (18.6).

title: Climate Gazette
text:
Climate Gazette features stories of extreme weather events that occurred in Europe over the past 40 years. Reports are based on data from the European Extreme Events Climate Index, analysed with Jupyter and presented via charts and maps.



 





Issue 1 - November 2026


Developed during the “E3CI Data Station: Visualising Extreme Weather for Decision-Makers and Communities” workshop held at the Visualising Climate Conference 2026, Bologna. Curated by Noemi Ambrosi, Simona Contaldi, and Cinzia Bongino.
